title: Guten Tag! Auf Wiedersehen! — formell vorstellen

paragraphs.text: Yesterday's scene was two strangers of the same age outside a building. This one is an office: three people, two of them strangers, all of them keeping the distance that German marks with {{de:Sie}}. Watch how much more formula the conversation carries — full greetings, full sentences, and a name given twice in two different ways.

Frau Weber opens with the time of day rather than with {{de:Hallo}}, introduces herself with {{de:Mein Name ist …}}, and Herr Hansen answers with the verb from the title of this page: {{de:Ich heiße Oliver Hansen}}. The same page, the same verb, two registers — that difference is the whole lesson.

Excuse me, what is your name? (formal)

paragraphs.text: Every German speaker decides this in the first two seconds of a conversation, and so do you. {{de:du}} is the close form: you use it with people your own age, with children, with anyone you have just called by their first name. {{de:Sie}} keeps the distance: your boss, a stranger at work, the woman you address as {{de:Frau Weber}} before you know her first name.

The clue is in the box at the bottom of the page. With {{de:du}} you give a first name — {{de:Ich heiße Nina}}. With {{de:Sie}} you give the whole name — {{de:Mein Name ist Nina Weber}} — and the question changes too: {{de:Wie heißt du?}} against {{de:Wie heißen Sie?}}. When in doubt at the very first meeting, take {{de:Sie}}; being politely too far away is a small mistake, and the other person will simply say {{de:du kannst mich duzen}} and pull you closer.
informell: du + Vorname — Wie heißt du? Wer bist du? · formell: Sie + Vorname + Nachname — Wie heißen Sie? Wie ist Ihr Name?
The question of wellbeing splits the same way. Friends say {{de:Wie geht's dir?}}; in the office you have heard {{de:Wie geht es Ihnen?}} — the same question, standing further back.

Two verbs carry this whole page, and each one changes its ending to match the person in front of it. The pronoun is the signal: {{de:ich}} takes {{de:-e}} or {{de:bin}}, {{de:du}} takes {{de:-st}} or {{de:bist}}, {{de:Sie}} takes {{de:-en}} or {{de:sind}}. You already heard all six forms in the dialogue above — the table is only putting the pattern on paper.
ich heiße · du heißt · Sie heißen
ich bin · du bist · Sie sind

Notice that {{de:heißen}} loses its double-s before the {{de:-t}} of {{de:du heißt}}, while {{de:Sie heißen}} happily keeps it. The stem decides, so learn the three forms as a block rather than one at a time.

blocks.englishBridge: English asks the same three questions without touching the verb at all — only the pronoun changes.
blocks.targetSentenceGerman: Wie heißen Sie? — Ich heiße Oliver Hansen.
